opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'm pretty skeptical of it, and I think a lot of that skepticism comes from spending forty years trying to get robots to do very simple things. There's this widespread assumption, especially in Silicon Valley, that everything is on an exponential curve: Moore's Law worked for transistors, so it must work for intelligence, for robotics, for everything. But the history of technology is full of curves that looked exponential for a while and then flattened out. They turned out to be S-curves. You get rapid progress, and then you hit some fundamental limit, and things slow way down.

Robotics is a really good example. People see the videos of humanoid robots doing backflips, or the huge leaps in language models, and they extrapolate. "If chatbots got this good in five years, robots will be folding our laundry and cooking dinner in another five." But manipulation, just picking things up reliably in an unstructured environment, has been incredibly hard. That's Moravec's paradox: things that are easy for a two-year-old, like grasping an unfamiliar object, are very hard for machines, while things we find hard, like chess or calculus, turn out to be relatively easy. The physical world has friction, uncertainty in sensing, uncertainty in control, deformable objects, all of it. And crucially, we don't have the internet-scale data for robot actions that we had for text. Language models trained on essentially everything humans have ever written. There's no equivalent dataset of robots touching and moving things. Some people estimate the gap is something like a hundred thousand years of data. So I don't think you can assume the same curve applies.

I also think the exponential framing feeds into the singularity idea, this notion that at some point machines surpass us and take off on their own. I've been arguing for a different idea I call "multiplicity": the future isn't machines replacing humans, it's diverse combinations of humans and machines working together on problems. That's what we actually see in practice. In surgery, in warehouses, in agriculture, the systems that work best are hybrid. The robot does the repetitive part and a human handles the edge cases.

To be fair, I don't want to be the guy who says progress isn't happening. It absolutely is, and some recent advances have genuinely surprised me. But I think we should be humble about prediction. Experts have consistently said "twenty years away" for many decades. My advice is to be excited about the progress but cautious about assuming it continues at the same rate forever. Nature tends to put the brakes on exponentials.

r001.rationale: The response warns that exponential trends often flatten into S-curves and rejects applying Moore’s Law broadly, but it does not clearly state that exponential growth is extremely rare in technological development.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'm a skeptic about that, and I think it's worth saying why, because the exponential story is so seductive. People point to Moore's law and say, look, this has held for fifty years, so of course everything else in technology must behave the same way. But Moore's law is really an anomaly. It's about one very specific thing, packing transistors onto silicon, and even that has been slowing down. It was never a law of nature. It was more like a self-fulfilling industry roadmap that happened to work for a remarkably long time.

In robotics, which is the world I live in, the curve looks nothing like that. I've been working on robot grasping for over thirty years, and the progress has been real but it's been slow and incremental. We still don't have a robot that can reliably clear a dinner table or fold laundry in an unfamiliar home. Every time we solve one problem, we uncover three more. That's not an exponential. If anything it's a long, grinding, roughly linear climb with occasional jumps when a new idea comes along, like deep learning did around 2012.

And I think the reason is that the physical world is just incredibly messy. Bits are clean. You can copy them perfectly, simulate them, scale them. Atoms don't cooperate like that. Friction, deformable objects, lighting, sensor noise, all of it resists the kind of clean scaling that software enjoys. Hans Moravec pointed this out decades ago: the things that are hard for humans, like chess, turned out to be easy for machines, and the things a two-year-old does effortlessly, like picking up a cup, are the hardest problems we have.

So my concern with the exponential framing isn't just that it's inaccurate. It's that it leads to a kind of boom-and-bust cycle. People get swept up in the hype, expectations run way ahead of reality, and then there's disappointment and funding dries up. We've seen that repeatedly in AI history. I'd rather we be honest about the pace, celebrate the genuine progress, and keep working steadily rather than promising things we can't deliver on a schedule.

r001.rationale: The response calls Moore’s law “an anomaly” tied to one specific technology and contrasts it with slow, incremental progress in robotics, conveying that exponential growth is exceptional in technological development.

astra-6.text:
I’m skeptical of treating exponential progress as a general law. We’ve seen extraordinary improvements in computing, and that can lead us to expect the same trajectory everywhere. But robotics involves the physical world, where progress can be much harder. Making a computer faster doesn’t automatically make a robot better at handling an unfamiliar object.

So I’d ask: what exactly are we measuring? Over what period? A particular technology can improve exponentially for a while, but that doesn’t mean the curve continues indefinitely, or that the capabilities we care about improve at the same rate. I’m optimistic about technological progress, but I think we should be cautious about extrapolating from a few impressive successes.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether exponential progress is a general law and cautions against extrapolation, but it does not state that exponential growth is extremely rare in technological development.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m skeptical of treating exponential progress as a general law. Moore’s law has been extraordinarily influential, and it’s tempting to extrapolate from that to technology as a whole. But computing power is one ingredient in a system. It doesn’t mean that the system’s capabilities improve at the same rate.

In robotics, for example, you have to contend with the physical world: uncertainty, friction, wear, and all the variations that are very difficult to anticipate. You can make a compelling demonstration, but getting a robot to do something reliably, day after day, is a much harder problem.

So I’d ask: What exactly are we measuring, and over what period? We can see very rapid progress in particular capabilities while other things remain stubbornly difficult. I’m excited about the progress, but I’m cautious about turning a particular trend into a prediction about everything.

r001.rationale: The candidate questions whether exponential progress is a general law and warns against extrapolating from Moore’s law, but it does not state that exponential growth is extremely rare in technological development.
